family.title: Grounded
family.text: Your folks have had it. Six nights of muddy sneakers, a phone that rang at 2 a.m. and a story about {villain} that nobody at the dinner table believes. You are grounded until Thanksgiving, and on Halloween night you watch Crystal Street from your bedroom window with the door locked from the outside. Down on the cul-de-sac the lights flicker, and something tall crosses the roundabout without you. Your crew does their best. In the morning a plate of pancakes appears outside your door, and after a long pause somebody knocks once and sits down in the hall to listen. It is a start. Next year, you tell them first.
family.art: A teenager in pajamas with their forehead pressed to a bedroom window on Halloween night, a locked door and a plate of untouched dinner behind them, far below on a suburban cul-de-sac flickering streetlights and a tall shadow crossing a roundabout garden

officials.title: Blamed
officials.text: Sheriff Dorsey has a clipboard, Vice Principal Kroll has a theory, and both of them have your name. Broken windows, a fire alarm, a ladder nobody can explain: every trace {villain} left this week is now officially your fault. On Halloween night you sit in the back of the sheriff's station drinking vending-machine cocoa while the town's real nightmare walks free. The deputy who drives you home stares at the purple glow over the roundabout for a long time and finally says, quietly, that she believes you. It does not fix the week. It is the first grown-up who listened.
officials.art: A teenager slumped on a bench in a small-town sheriff's station at night holding a paper cup of cocoa, a clipboard and a stack of incident reports on the desk, a deputy at the window watching a purple glow over the suburban rooftops

neighbors.title: Run Out of the Cul-de-Sac
neighbors.text: It starts with casseroles left on your porch with notes that say WE KNOW. It ends with the Neighborhood Watch on your lawn in bathrobes, holding flashlights and one rolling pin, demanding that whatever is wrong with Crystal Street go somewhere else, starting with you. You spend Halloween night at your aunt's apartment across town, eating candy corn and watching the late movie, while {villain} has the cul-de-sac to itself. By Thanksgiving the Watch quietly stops meeting. Mrs. Delgado brings back your bike with a new bell and an apology she cannot quite say out loud.
neighbors.art: A crowd of suburban neighbors in bathrobes and curlers on a front lawn at night holding flashlights, a rolling pin and casserole dishes, a teenager on the porch with a backpack, Halloween pumpkins on the steps and a purple glow behind the houses

final-girl.title: Final Girl
final-girl.text: Everyone else went home, or got scared, or got shaken loose one bad night at a time, and so it came down to you, alone on Crystal Street with {villain}. And you won. Not because you were the good one or the pure one or the one the script picked, but because you knew the rules and you refused to run upstairs. At dawn your crew finds you on the curb with a flashlight that is out of batteries and a grin that is not, and somebody solemnly pins a hand-lettered paper badge to your jacket: FINAL GIRL. It is a title, not a gender. {name} earned it.
final-girl.art: A teenager sitting on a suburban curb at dawn holding a dead flashlight, jacket torn, grinning, a hand-drawn paper badge pinned to the jacket, a crowd of relieved friends running toward them down a cul-de-sac strewn with Halloween debris
